title: Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
official_title: Making further continuing appropriations and other extensions for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-4 on March 15, 2025. This was the full-year measure that funded the federal government for the rest of fiscal year 2025 and averted a shutdown after the prior stopgap expired.

votes.question: On Passage of the Bill H.R. 1968

summary: Funds the federal government for the rest of fiscal year 2025 (through September 30, 2025) by continuing fiscal year 2024 appropriations, but with the Department of Defense funded at new line-item levels and given added flexibility while most nondefense agencies stay at prior-year amounts. It also extends a set of expiring health programs — community health centers, telehealth, and several Medicare and Medicaid provisions — and a handful of other authorities.
brief: Full-year stopgap funding the government through September 30, 2025: continues FY2024 levels, sets new defense amounts, and extends expiring health programs.

top_lines.headline: Full-Year Funding Through September 30, 2025
subs: Continues fiscal year 2024 appropriations for most of the government for the rest of FY2025
Funds run through September 30, 2025, replacing the expiring short-term stopgap
Strips out the earmarks (community project funding) that were carried in the FY2024 bills

top_lines.headline: Defense Funded in Full; Nondefense Held Flat
subs: Sets specific, account-by-account funding levels for the Department of Defense rather than simply continuing prior-year amounts
Most nondefense agencies remain at FY2024 levels, an effective cut after inflation
Requires agencies to submit detailed FY2025 spending plans and OMB to report monthly on obligations

top_lines.headline: Health Program Extensions
subs: Extends funding for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and teaching health centers through September 30, 2025
Extends Medicare telehealth flexibilities and hospital-at-home authority and delays Medicaid DSH payment cuts
Extends the temporary scheduling order for fentanyl-related substances through September 30, 2025

items.main: Continues fiscal year 2024 funding levels, authorities, and conditions for most of the government.
items.detail: Appropriates, for the listed FY2024 appropriations Acts, the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions, for projects and activities not otherwise specifically provided for. It applies to all twelve appropriations subcommittees' bills, subject to specific exceptions and dollar substitutions ('anomalies') spelled out account by account.

items.main: Sets the funding to run through the end of fiscal year 2025.
items.detail: Unless otherwise provided, appropriations and authority under the division are available through September 30, 2025.

items.main: Nullifies the earmarks that were attached to the FY2024 appropriations.
items.detail: Provides that any language specifying an earmark in an FY2024 appropriations Act, or in an accompanying committee report or joint explanatory statement, has no legal effect for funds appropriated by the division. 'Earmark' is defined by reference to House Rule XXI and Senate Rule XLIV (congressional earmarks, community project funding, congressionally directed spending).

items.main: Requires departments and agencies to submit detailed FY2025 operating plans.
items.detail: Within 45 days of enactment, each of the listed departments and agencies must submit to the Appropriations Committees a spending, expenditure, or operating plan at the program, project, or activity level (or, for foreign assistance, by country and program). Section 1114 separately requires OMB to report monthly, from May 15 through November 1, 2025, on obligations by account compared to the same period in FY2024.

items.main: Sets specific dollar levels for Defense accounts instead of simply continuing prior-year funding.
items.detail: Notwithstanding the general continuing-appropriations rule, the division specifies funding account by account for the Department of Defense — for example, $51.18B for Military Personnel, Army and $73.66B for Operation and Maintenance, Navy — and provides new line-item procurement and research figures. This gives the Pentagon updated amounts and reprogramming room that the rest of the government, held at FY2024 levels, does not get.

sections.label: Section 2101 — Community Health Center and Workforce Extensions

items.main: Extends mandatory funding for community health centers and related workforce programs through September 30, 2025.
items.detail: Amends the Affordable Care Act and Public Health Service Act to add $2.14B for community health centers, $172.97M for the National Health Service Corps, and $87.74M for teaching health centers that operate graduate medical education programs, each for the period April 1 through September 30, 2025.

items.main: Extends the Special Diabetes Program and the Special Diabetes Program for Indians.
items.detail: Adds $79.83M for each program for the period April 1 through September 30, 2025, to remain available until expended.

items.main: Extends the pandemic-era Medicare telehealth flexibilities by six months.
items.detail: Pushes the expiration of multiple telehealth provisions in the Social Security Act from March 31, 2025 to September 30, 2025 — including the removal of geographic and originating-site restrictions, the expanded list of eligible practitioners, audio-only services, telehealth for federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics, and the delay of in-person requirements for tele-mental-health.

items.main: Increases the Medicare Improvement Fund balance.
items.detail: Amends section 1898(b)(1) of the Social Security Act to change the fund amount from $1.25B to $1.80B.

items.main: Delays scheduled cuts to Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital payments.
items.detail: Amends section 1923(f)(7)(A) of the Social Security Act to remove the reduction for the April 1 through September 30, 2025 period and to extend the schedule of reductions through fiscal year 2028 instead of 2027.

items.main: Extends the temporary class-wide scheduling of fentanyl-related substances.
items.detail: Amends the Temporary Reauthorization and Study of the Emergency Scheduling of Fentanyl Analogues Act to push the order's expiration from March 31, 2025 to September 30, 2025.

items.main: Exempts the health and other-matters divisions from PAYGO scorecards.
items.detail: Provides that the budgetary effects of divisions B and C are not entered on the statutory or Senate PAYGO scorecards.

criticisms.why: I rise to oppose this cruel betrayal of America's veterans, seniors, and working families. This 1-year CR doesn't make rent or healthcare bills more affordable, which is what keeps my constituents up at night. Instead, it actually cuts housing aid that could force 32,000 veterans, domestic violence survivors, seniors, and people with disabilities into homelessness. What does this spending patch do as we all now stare down the barrel of another Trump recession?

and still I rise, to oppose a Continuing Resolution that will allow a chainsaw to, among other things: minimize Medicaid with underfunded block grants to states, marginalize Medicare's ``Dual Eligibles'' long-term Medicaid care, and privatize Social Security by allowing private investment of Social Security funds in the stock market with no protections from market downturns. Mr. Speaker, the costs of the cuts in spending will be measurable. However, the human cost in pain and suffering will be immeasurable.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Wasserman Schultz
featured_quotes.text: I rise to oppose this cruel betrayal of America's veterans, seniors, and working families. This 1-year CR doesn't make rent or healthcare bills more affordable, which is what keeps my constituents up at night. Instead, it actually cuts housing aid that could force 32,000 veterans, domestic violence survivors, seniors, and people with disabilities into homelessness. What does this spending patch do as we all now stare down the barrel of another Trump recession?

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Green
featured_quotes.text: and still I rise, to oppose a Continuing Resolution that will allow a chainsaw to, among other things: minimize Medicaid with underfunded block grants to states, marginalize Medicare's ``Dual Eligibles'' long-term Medicaid care, and privatize Social Security by allowing private investment of Social Security funds in the stock market with no protections from market downturns. Mr. Speaker, the costs of the cuts in spending will be measurable. However, the human cost in pain and suffering will be immeasurable.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rutherford
featured_quotes.text: I really appreciate all the hard work that got us here today. Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you, as I sat here on this floor listening to the conversation, it reminded me of an old saying that my father had. For many, many years, I heard this: A lie can travel around the world three times before the truth can get up and put its pants on. That was before the internet. Now, after what I have heard today, I would say it is probably more like 100 times that a lie can travel around the world before the truth can get up and put its pants on.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Bice
featured_quotes.text: I think my colleagues on the other side of the aisle are confused about what is in this bill and what is not. They keep talking about impacts to mandatory spending, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. That is not in this bill. Just because you keep repeating the same dishonest talking points doesn't make it true. This legislation continues funding and prevents a government shutdown, which would have a devastating impact on my home State of Oklahoma and communities across the country.
